newsitem.title: USA: Congress, W.House reach pact on DC revitalization.
newsitem.headline: Congress, W.House reach pact on DC revitalization.

text.p: Congressional negotiators have agreed on "core parts" of President Clinton's proposed multi-billion dollar revitalization plan for the District of Columbia, OMB Director Franklin Raines announced Wednesday.

"All in all, this is a major success for the District," Raines told reporters at a press briefing to announce a broad agreement designed to strengthen the city's economic base and relieve it of major financial and managerial burdens.
The plan was agreed to by congressional leaders at roughly 0300 EDT Wednesday morning, Raines said.

It includes tax incentives to stimulate D.C. business development, tackles the city's cash shortfall, provides access to tax-exempt financing in poverty areas and shifts pension and other financial responsibilities now borne by D.C. to the federal government, Raines said.

Specifically, the agreement provides a 20 percent tax credit for the first $15,000 of wages that employers pay to workers living and working in sections of D.C. with at least 20 percent poverty, Raines said.

The plan provides a $5,000 tax credit for first-time homebuyers in the city. The credit would be phased out for joint filers with incomes between $110,000 and $130,000 and singles earning between $70,000 and $90,000, Raines said.
There would be zero taxation on capital gains for businesses that get at least 80 percent of their gross income from areas of the city with 10 percent poverty, Raines said.

The plan also provides access to tax-exempt financing in poverty areas, Raines said. And it allows the District to borrow up to $300 million from the U.S. Treasury, with a maturity of up to 10 years, Raines said.
Currently, the District gets a $660 million annual federal payment in lieu of taxes from Congress for the federal government's extensive use of District facilities.
The new agreement provides for a one-time federal contribution of $190 million in 1998, but the federal payment is eliminated after that, Raines said.

"This is the most important legislation for the District of Columbia in the 20th century, other than the Home Rule (law)," Eleanor Holmes Norton, the city's delegate to Congress said at a press briefing..

In other key provisions, the federal government now assumes the city's roughly $5 billion pension liability under the plan and the federal share of Medicaid payments rises from the current 50 percent to 70 percent, Raines said.
And the U.S. Bureau of Prison will take responsibility for all sentenced felons now living at Lorton Correctional Facility, which will close December 31, 2001, Raines said.
